title: Workspaces
text:
Sharing a Workspace
Only Owners can share. In the workspace, click Share (top right), then:

Enter your collaborator’s email: the one linked to their Workbench account
Choose their role: Owner, Writer, or Reader


They must already have a Workbench account. You can’t invite someone who hasn’t registered yet.
They get access to the resources you created in the workspace (buckets, datasets), at their role’s level
References to outside data are not shared automatically. The data’s owner has to grant access.
With a group policy, only group members can open it. You won’t be warned if you share with someone outside the group.







TipInstructor tip





For All of Us workspaces, collaborators also need their own All of Us data access (Registered or Controlled Tier) to see the data collection. Verily recommends sharing with Workbench groups rather than individuals for larger teams; that’s beyond what students need here.

section: Snippets Are Gone: Use Your Bucket Folder
text:
Snippets Are Gone: Use Your Bucket Folder
Classic Workbench: copy files to and from the workspace bucket with code snippets (e.g., copy_file_from_workspace_bucket.R) that ran gsutil
Workbench 2.0: no Snippets menu. Your buckets are automatically mounted as folders in every app:
/home/jupyter/workspace/<bucket name>/     standard apps (JupyterLab, R, SAS)
/home/dataproc/workspace/<bucket name>/    Spark (Dataproc) apps
So you save and read files with regular R or Python functions, as if the bucket were a local folder. (No bucket yet? See New Cloud Storage Bucket.)

Your own buckets: read and write
References, including data collection buckets (e.g., v9-genomics-folder): read-only. Don’t save outputs there.







TipInstructor tip





If you put a resource inside a folder on the Resources tab, the folder becomes part of the path (use quotes if the folder name has spaces). Mounts don’t update on their own: a bucket you add (or rename) after the app starts won’t show up until you restart the app or run wb resource mount (or wb resource mount –id= for one). A folder ending in _NO_ACCESS, _NOT_FOUND, or _MOUNT_FAILED means that mount failed. Duplicated workspaces keep their mounts. Source: Verily, “Access workspace files and folders”.

title: Storage & Costs
text:
Saving and Reading Files
R
bucket <- file.path(Sys.getenv("HOME"), "workspace", "workspace-bucket")

readr::write_csv(clean_df, file.path(bucket, "clean_data.csv"))   # save
clean_df <- readr::read_csv(file.path(bucket, "clean_data.csv"))  # read
Python
import os, pandas as pd
bucket = os.path.expanduser("~/workspace/workspace-bucket")

clean_df.to_csv(f"{bucket}/clean_data.csv", index=False)   # save
clean_df = pd.read_csv(f"{bucket}/clean_data.csv")         # read






TipInstructor tip





Replace workspace-bucket with your bucket’s name as shown in the Resources tab. HOME / ~ points to /home/jupyter or /home/dataproc depending on the app, so this code works in both. The folder tree under ~/workspace matches the folders in the Resources tab. Apps use a standard disk, so files saved anywhere else on the app (e.g., the home directory) are lost if the app crashes or is deleted.

The CDR dataset path is in the queries Data Explorer generates (the FROM clause), and in the data collection’s BigQuery resources on the Resources tab.

title: Storage & Costs
text:
Storage

Workspace bucket: shared, permanent, and the cheapest option for long-term storage. Recommended. (You create it; see New Cloud Storage Bucket.)
App disk: attached to an app. Charged until the app is deleted, even when stopped. Files on it survive Stop but are lost on Delete.







TipInstructor tip





See What is an app? and Reading the cost estimate on the Apps page.

title: Storage & Costs
text:
Saving Money

Save your data to workspace storage
Stop or delete apps you aren’t using; keep autostop on
Your notebooks and data in workspace storage stay intact
Start a new app any time to pick up where you left off
Delete workspaces you no longer need

⚠️ Deleting a workspace permanently deletes everything created in it, including your bucket and its files. It can’t be undone. Copy anything you need first.






TipInstructor tip





Only Owners can delete a workspace. References (e.g., the All of Us data collection) are only pointers, so the underlying data isn’t affected.

title: Overview and Resources Tabs
text:
Buckets, Objects, Datasets, and Tables


Cloud Storage: files
bucket      my-workspace-bucket
└── object  data/results.csv

A bucket is a container; an object is one file in it
Address: gs://my-workspace-bucket/data/results.csv
Folders aren’t real: data/ is just the start of the file’s name, so an empty folder disappears



BigQuery: tables
project         wb-silky-artichoke-2408
└── dataset     C2025Q4R6
    └── table   person

A dataset is a collection of tables; a table has rows and columns
Address: project.dataset.table, used in SQL after FROM
You pay for the data a query reads, so select only the columns you need



👉 All of Us data uses both: tables in BigQuery (EHR, surveys, measurements) and files in a bucket (genomic and multi-omics data).






TipInstructor tip





Example: the Controlled Tier v9 tables are the dataset C2025Q4R6, which the notebooks call CURRENT_DATASET; the genomic files are objects in the vwb-aou-datasets-controlled bucket, mounted in apps under ~/workspace/. The Workbench and the Google Cloud console show object names containing “/” as folders to make browsing easier. Don’t confuse these with the Workbench’s New Folder resource (next section): that is only a label for grouping resources on the Resources tab, and its dialog says “Folders don’t affect cloud paths”.

Description (optional)

Click Create folder

Folders don’t change a resource’s cloud path (gs://…), but they do appear in the app’s mounted path: ~/workspace/<folder>/<bucket>

title: Overview and Resources Tabs
text:
New Cloud Storage Bucket










Why: new workspaces have no bucket, and you need one to save your work

Resource ID: the name inside Workbench (letters, numbers, -, _). The tutorials use workspace-bucket.
Folder path and Description
Bucket name: the name in Google Cloud. It must be globally unique, so keep the generated one: your Resource ID + the workspace’s project ID (↻ makes a new one).

Click Create bucket. You can use it right away; collaborators may wait up to 15 min.








TipInstructor tip





Controlled resources like this bucket are shared with workspace collaborators and deleted when the workspace is deleted. Apps that were already running won’t see a new bucket until you restart the app or run wb resource mount. Mounted folders cache file info for about a minute, so two people writing at once may not see each other’s changes right away. Migrated 1.0 workspaces already have a bucket: rw-migration-aou-rw-…

title: Overview and Resources Tabs
text:
Bucket Names: Good Practice

Lowercase letters, numbers, -, _, 3–63 characters, no spaces, no “google”
Bucket names are public: anyone can check whether a name exists

⚠️ No names, emails, NetIDs, or project details

A bucket name can’t be changed (the resource’s name and description can). To rename, create a new bucket and copy the files over.
Deleting a bucket frees its name for anyone to reuse

👉 Easiest: accept the generated name. It’s built from your Resource ID + the workspace’s project ID, so keep the Resource ID free of personal details too.






TipInstructor tip





Source: Google Cloud, “About Cloud Storage buckets” and “Create a bucket”. Files (objects) also can’t be renamed in place; renaming copies and deletes them. Avoid putting sensitive information in file names too.

text:
New BigQuery Dataset










Why: save large query results as tables, then query them again with SQL instead of re-running long queries or loading big CSVs

Resource ID, Folder path, Description
Dataset ID: the name in Google Cloud. Unique within your project; letters, numbers, _ only. Keep the generated one or choose your own. Can’t be changed later.

Click Create dataset. Collaborators may wait up to 15 min.








TipInstructor tip





Optional for most class projects; a bucket with CSV files is usually enough. BigQuery storage and queries are billed to your pod.

title: Overview and Resources Tabs
text:
Referencing Existing Data
A reference points to data that already exists elsewhere. Nothing is copied.







Reference
You’ll need




Cloud Storage bucket
The bucket name


Cloud Storage object (one file)
Its URL, e.g., gs://bucket-name/path/file.csv


BigQuery dataset
Project ID + Dataset ID


BigQuery table
Project ID + Dataset ID + Table ID



Every reference also has a Resource ID, Folder path, and Description. Then click Add to resources.
⚠️ Access isn’t shared automatically. The data’s owner controls it. In a Controlled Tier workspace, the perimeter may also block data from outside it.






TipInstructor tip





Example uses: point to a collaborator’s bucket, or to a shared file without copying it. The All of Us data collection resources you added earlier are references too. Deleting a reference removes the pointer, not the data. You can edit a reference’s name and description, but not the bucket name, project ID, dataset ID, or table ID; to fix those, delete the reference and add it again. Some outside buckets are “Requester Pays”: reading or browsing them is billed to your pod, and mounting them when an app starts can cost money too. The Workbench shows a warning when you add one.

title: Overview and Resources Tabs
text:
Getting and Reusing Data
Someone else’s data. A gs:// address says where data is, not that you may read it. The owner has to give you access:

Share the workspace (the expected route for All of Us data): the owner clicks Share and adds you as Reader or Writer. You get the buckets and datasets they created there, and you need your own All of Us access at the same tier.
A bucket outside a shared workspace: the owner grants your account access, then you add a reference to it.
References inside a shared workspace aren’t passed on: the original data’s owner has to grant access separately.

Your own data from another workspace: add a reference to that workspace’s bucket or dataset. Limits:

⚠️ Controlled Tier data, or anything made from it, can’t go to a Registered Tier workspace or outside the perimeter
⚠️ Person IDs changed between v8 and v9: files saved from v8 (or the classic Workbench) can’t be joined to v9 data
⚠️ Each workspace is one project with its own Research Use Statement: check with All of Us support before reusing participant-level results in another project







TipInstructor tip





To confirm before teaching: the exact Verily steps for granting someone access to a single bucket (Verily resource settings or Google Cloud permissions), and All of Us’s rule on reusing participant-level results across projects. Between two of your Controlled Tier workspaces, references should work, but the perimeter is enforced per workspace, so test with a small file first. For classes, rerunning the queries in each workspace is simplest. Source for the v8 to v9 ID change: CDR v9 release, All of Us Office Hours, 2026-07-24.

title: Apps
text:
Managing your app
On the Apps tab:







Action
What happens




Open
Click the app’s name (when it’s Running)


Stop
Stops it right away, with no confirmation. Computing charges stop; disk charges continue.


Start
Restarts a stopped app in about a minute


Edit
Name, description, and autostop: any time. Machine type and disk: only when stopped.


Delete
Removes the app and its disk. ⚠️ Anything not saved in a bucket is lost.









TipInstructor tip





You can’t change an app’s image (app type) or instance name; create a new app instead. Apps that are Starting or Stopping can’t be changed until they finish. If someone loses Writer access to the workspace, their apps are stopped (“abandoned”); an Owner can restore the access or delete the app.

text:
⚠️ Read this first: data protection
Everything you push to a public GitHub repo can be seen by anyone, and you can’t fully take it back once it’s pushed.
The All of Us Data and Statistics Dissemination Policy prohibits sharing:

Participant-level data of any kind
Aggregate counts or statistics based on 1–20 participants (this includes notebook outputs, tables, and plots)

Share code, not results. Before every push:

Clear notebook outputs (the command is in the steps below).
Leave out data files (.csv, .tsv, .parquet, .vcf, etc.).
Check for credentials (tokens, keys, passwords).
Run git status and look at every file before committing.

Check the current policy on the All of Us Research Hub if you’re unsure about anything.

title: GitHub Guide
text:
Before you start
You need:

An All of Us workspace on Verily Workbench
A GitHub account
For Path A: write access to the existing repo (ask the repo or organization owner to add you)

You do not need to install anything on your own computer. Everything happens in a terminal inside a Workbench app, where the Workbench CLI (wb) and Git are already installed and you’re already logged in.

title: GitHub Guide
section: Step 1: Start an app and open a terminal
text:
Step 1: Start an app and open a terminal

In your workspace, go to the Apps tab and create an app.

AoU Jupyter is the simplest choice for Git work.
Avoid JupyterLab Spark cluster for AoU unless you need Spark. It costs more and starts slower.
R Analysis Environment for AoU also works. Use RStudio’s Terminal tab.

Once the app is running, open it.
Open a terminal: File → New → Terminal, or the Terminal tile in the Launcher (+ tab).
Confirm you’re logged in:

wb auth status

Tip: If you add a Git repo to the workspace (Apps tab → Git repositories → + Add repository) before creating the app, the app clones it automatically. Apps created earlier won’t get it. Clone it manually as shown below.

title: GitHub Guide
section: Step 2: Connect Workbench to GitHub (one-time setup)
text:
Step 2: Connect Workbench to GitHub (one-time setup)

2a. Test the connection
cd ~
ssh -T git@github.com
The first time, you may be asked Are you sure you want to continue connecting (yes/no)?. Type yes.

✅ Success looks like: Hi YOUR-USERNAME! You've successfully authenticated, but GitHub does not provide shell access. (The “no shell access” part is normal.) Skip to 2c.
❌ Permission denied (publickey) means GitHub doesn’t know your key yet. Continue to 2b.



2b. Add your Workbench SSH key to GitHub
Get your public key:
wb security ssh-key get
If that errors because no key exists, run wb security ssh-key generate first.
Then, on GitHub:

Click your profile picture → Settings → SSH and GPG keys → New SSH key
Title: Verily Workbench. Key type: Authentication Key
Paste the whole key line (starting with ssh-rsa or similar) → Add SSH key
If a Configure SSO button appears next to the key, click it and authorize your organization.

Run ssh -T git@github.com again to confirm.


2c. Set your Git identity
⚠️ Replace the example values with your own. Don’t paste them as-is.
git config --global user.name "your-github-username"
git config --global user.email "your-email@example.com"
git config --global --list    # confirm what's set
For a public repo, consider using your GitHub noreply email so your real address isn’t published. Find it at GitHub Settings → Emails. It looks like 12345678+username@users.noreply.github.com.

title: GitHub Guide
text:
Step 3: Find your notebooks
Your workspace notebooks are usually in a mounted bucket folder like:
/home/jupyter/workspace/<your-workspace-folder>/notebooks
List them:
ls -la /home/jupyter/workspace/<your-workspace-folder>/notebooks
Save any open notebooks in JupyterLab first (Ctrl/Cmd+S) so you copy the latest version.

Important: Do not run git init or git clone inside ~/workspace/.... It’s a mounted cloud bucket, and Git doesn’t work well there. Always clone into your home directory (~) and copy files over.

title: GitHub Guide
section: Path A: Add your work to an existing repo
text:
Path A: Add your work to an existing repo

A1. Clone the repo and create a branch
Use the repo’s SSH URL (green Code button on GitHub → SSH):
cd ~
git clone git@github.com:OWNER/REPO-NAME.git
cd REPO-NAME
git checkout -b add-my-notebooks
The cloned folder is named after the repo (REPO-NAME).


A2. Copy in your notebooks
Put them in a subfolder so they don’t clash with existing files:
mkdir -p notebooks
cp /home/jupyter/workspace/<your-workspace-folder>/notebooks/*.ipynb notebooks/
ls notebooks/

To use an existing folder or a name with spaces, use quotes: mkdir -p "Session 3" and cp ... "Session 3/"
To copy a single file whose name has spaces, quote the full path: cp "/home/jupyter/workspace/<folder>/notebooks/01. my notebook.ipynb" notebooks/



A3. Clean before committing
# Remove all outputs (keeps code and markdown)
jupyter nbconvert --clear-output --inplace notebooks/*.ipynb

# Check for credentials
grep -iE "token|key|secret|password" notebooks/*.ipynb
If the grep prints anything that looks like a credential, edit or remove that file before continuing. Pay special attention to notebooks that load environment variables or configuration.


A4. Commit and push
git status                     # review every file listed
git add notebooks
git commit -m "Add analysis notebooks from All of Us workspace"
git push -u origin add-my-notebooks


A5. Open and merge a pull request
The push doesn’t change main by itself. You need to merge your branch through a pull request:

Go to the repo on GitHub.
Click the yellow Compare & pull request banner. (If it’s not there: Pull requests tab → New pull request, with base: main and compare: add-my-notebooks.)
Check the Files changed tab. It should contain only the files you meant to add.
Click Create pull request, then Merge pull request → Confirm merge.
Optionally click Delete branch.



A6. Update your local copy
git checkout main
git pull

title: GitHub Guide
section: Path B: Create a new repo for your work
text:
Path B: Create a new repo for your work

B1. Create an empty repo on GitHub

On GitHub, click + (top right) → New repository.
Choose a name and set it to Public or Private.
Don’t add a README, .gitignore, or license. Leave it empty to avoid conflicts on the first push.
Click Create repository and copy the SSH URL.



B2. Set up the repo in your home directory
mkdir -p ~/my-new-repo/notebooks
cd ~/my-new-repo
git init
git branch -M main
git remote add origin git@github.com:YOUR-USERNAME/my-new-repo.git


B3. Copy, clean, and add a .gitignore
cp /home/jupyter/workspace/<your-workspace-folder>/notebooks/*.ipynb notebooks/
jupyter nbconvert --clear-output --inplace notebooks/*.ipynb
grep -iE "token|key|secret|password" notebooks/*.ipynb

# Keep data files and clutter out of Git
cat > .gitignore << 'EOF'
*.csv
*.tsv
*.parquet
*.vcf
*.vcf.gz
*.bam
*.rds
*.RData
.ipynb_checkpoints/
.DS_Store
EOF
Optionally create a README.md describing the project, the order to run the notebooks in, and what data access is required.


B4. First commit and push
git status
git add .
git commit -m "Initial commit: analysis notebooks"
git push -u origin main
No pull request is needed here. The files go straight to main.

title: GitHub Guide
section: Finding your repo in the JupyterLab file browser
text:
Finding your repo in the JupyterLab file browser
The file browser often opens inside your workspace’s notebooks folder, so the repo you cloned to ~ won’t be visible at first. Click the folder icon at the start of the path bar to jump to the top level, and your repo folder will be there.
/home/jupyter/                      ← top level
├── REPO-NAME/                      ← your Git repo (synced with GitHub)
│   └── notebooks/
└── workspace/
    └── <your-workspace-folder>/
        └── notebooks/              ← your original copies (NOT in Git)

title: GitHub Guide
text:
Ongoing workflow: keeping in sync
After setup, work from the repo folder (~/REPO-NAME/notebooks/), not the original workspace folder.
Each session:
cd ~/REPO-NAME
git checkout main
git pull                       # get the latest from GitHub
# ...edit and run notebooks...
jupyter nbconvert --clear-output --inplace notebooks/*.ipynb
git status
git add notebooks
git commit -m "Describe your change"
git push
You can push straight to main if it’s your own repo, or use a branch and pull request (as in Path A) if others should review first.
Things to know:

There are two copies of your notebooks. git pull updates only the repo copy, not the originals in ~/workspace/.... Pick the repo copy as your working copy, or the two will drift apart.
Pulled notebooks have no outputs because you cleared them. Rerun the cells to regenerate results.
The clone lives on the app’s disk. If you delete the app, the clone goes with it. Always push before deleting an app, then clone again in the new one.
New apps need setup. In a new app, you may need to repeat git config (Step 2c) and clone the repo again.

title: GitHub Guide
text:
Sharing with colleagues
To use your code in their own All of Us workspace, colleagues run:
cd ~
git clone https://github.com/OWNER/REPO-NAME.git
No SSH key is needed to clone a public repo over HTTPS. They need the same data access tier your notebooks use (e.g., Controlled Tier).
To contribute back, colleagues need:

Write access to the repo (granted by the repo or organization owner)
Their own Workbench SSH key added to their GitHub account (Step 2b)
To clone with the git@github.com:... URL

Make notebooks portable: avoid hardcoded workspace paths. Build paths from your home folder, and keep the bucket name and dataset path in one place at the top of the notebook, so collaborators only change those lines:
# R
bucket <- file.path(Sys.getenv("HOME"), "workspace", "workspace-bucket")  # your bucket's name
CURRENT_DATASET <- "<project-id>.<dataset-id>"   # copy from your Data Explorer query
# Python
import os
bucket = os.path.expanduser("~/workspace/workspace-bucket")  # your bucket's name
CURRENT_DATASET = "<project-id>.<dataset-id>"   # copy from your Data Explorer query
WORKSPACE_BUCKET and WORKSPACE_CDR from the classic Workbench are not set in new Workbench 2.0 workspaces (see Workspace Variables).
To share results, share the workspace itself through Workbench’s sharing settings so data and outputs stay inside All of Us.

title: GitHub Guide
text:
Troubleshooting








Problem / message
What it means
Fix




“I don’t see a terminal app” when creating an app
There isn’t a separate terminal app
Terminals are inside each app. In JupyterLab: File → New → Terminal. In RStudio: Terminal tab.


fatal: not a git repository ... Stopping at filesystem boundary
You’re in a folder that isn’t a Git repo, often the mounted ~/workspace bucket
Normal before cloning. cd ~ and clone there. Don’t git init inside ~/workspace.


Permission denied (publickey)
GitHub doesn’t recognize a key from this app
Add your key from wb security ssh-key get to GitHub (Step 2b). If it still fails, run ls -la ~/.ssh. If the key is missing, restart the app, or create one with ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -f ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 -N "" and add ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub to GitHub.


You've successfully authenticated, but GitHub does not provide shell access
This is success
Nothing to fix. Carry on.


ERROR: Repository not found or Permission ... denied on push
Your account doesn’t have write access, or the URL is wrong
Check the URL with git remote -v. Ask the owner for write access, or fork the repo and push to your fork.


An error mentioning SAML SSO
Your organization requires SSO authorization for keys
GitHub Settings → SSH and GPG keys → Configure SSO on the Workbench key → authorize the org.


Commits show the wrong name or email (e.g., “Your Name”)
Placeholder values were used in git config
Rerun git config --global user.name/user.email with your real values. Check with git config --global --list.


destination path 'REPO-NAME' already exists
You already cloned it (or the app auto-cloned it)
Skip git clone and cd into the folder. Find it with find ~ -maxdepth 3 -type d -name "REPO-NAME".


Config option 'extra_template_paths' not recognized during nbconvert
Harmless warning
Ignore it. Outputs are still cleared.


Pushed, but files don’t show on GitHub’s main page
They’re on your branch, not on main
Create and merge a pull request (Step A5), or switch to your branch in GitHub’s branch dropdown to see them.


“Where’s my pull request?”
Pull requests aren’t created automatically
Click Compare & pull request on the repo page after pushing.


Can’t find the cloned repo in the JupyterLab file browser
The browser is showing a subfolder of ~/workspace
Click the folder icon at the start of the path bar to go to the top level.


No such file or directory with a filename containing spaces
The shell split the name at the spaces
Wrap the path in quotes: "01. my notebook.ipynb".


git pull refuses because of local changes
You have uncommitted edits to files that also changed on GitHub
git status, then commit your changes or discard them with git restore <file>, then pull again.


Merge conflict in a .ipynb file
Two people edited the same notebook
Notebooks are JSON and hard to merge. Keep one person per notebook where possible. To keep one side entirely: git checkout --ours <file> or git checkout --theirs <file>, then git add and commit.


Repo added to the workspace but not in my app
The app was created before the repo was added
In the app terminal: wb git clone --resource=<resource-name>, or git clone <url>.


Accidentally pushed outputs or data
Sensitive content is now on GitHub
Act quickly: make the repo private if possible, remove the content, and contact the All of Us support team about the policy steps. Deleting it in a new commit does not remove it from Git history.

text:
Setting Up Your Environment (R)
The tutorial’s setup script defines your workspace variables:
source("/home/jupyter/workspace/aou-tutorial-notebooks/Setting_Env_Variables_p2.R")

library(bigrquery)
library(tidyverse)

CURRENT_DATASET <- Sys.getenv("WORKSPACE_CDR")   # the CDR in this workspace

download_data <- function(query) {
  tb <- bq_project_query(Sys.getenv("GOOGLE_PROJECT"), query)
  bq_table_download(tb)
}

The script sets WORKSPACE_BUCKET and WORKSPACE_CDR. Without it, they don’t exist (see Workspace Variables).
The All of Us app image in 2.0 is smaller, so you may need to install packages
In a migrated workspace, set WORKSPACE_BUCKET to your migration bucket (gs://rw-migration-…)

title: Tutorial Workspaces
text:
Updating SQL Queries
Replace hard-coded 1.0 dataset paths with CURRENT_DATASET:
1.0: won’t run ❌
query <- str_glue("SELECT * FROM `fc-aou-cdr-prod-ct.C2024Q3R8.condition_occurrence` LIMIT 5")
2.0: runs ✅
query <- str_glue("SELECT * FROM `{CURRENT_DATASET}.condition_occurrence` LIMIT 5")
df <- download_data(query)
The standard OMOP tables (condition_occurrence, person, measurement…) keep their names. Only the path changes.

text:
Inside the Exported R Notebook
The notebook has the SQL for each table, plus code to run it:
Sys.setenv(EXPORT_BUCKET = "gs://<your-bucket-name>")   # ⚠️ not set for you

bq_table_save(                                  # run the query (billed to your project)...
  bq_dataset_query("<data project>.<index dataset>", person_sql,
                   billing = "<your workspace project>"),
  person_path, destination_format = "CSV")      # ...and save it as CSVs in your bucket

title: Omics for Beginners
section: The big picture: DNA → RNA → protein
text:
The big picture: DNA → RNA → protein
Think of a cell as a kitchen:










In the kitchen
In the cell
Measured in All of Us by




DNA
the cookbook: every recipe, the same in every kitchen of the house
all the instructions, the same in nearly every cell, fixed from birth
whole-genome sequencing, genotyping arrays (classes 4.1–4.4)


RNA
a photocopy of one recipe, made when it’s needed
a working copy of one gene; more copies = a more active gene
RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) of blood (class 4.5)


Protein
the dish that gets made
the product: hormones, enzymes, signals
Olink proteomics, blood plasma (class 4.6)



DNA ──(copied)──→ RNA ──(translated)──→ protein
fixed             changes with          changes with
from birth        time, disease,        time, disease,
                  medicines             medicines
This is why the classes ask different questions of each layer:

DNA tells you about lifelong risk: a variant you’re born with can’t be caused by diabetes. That makes genetic results useful for asking about cause.
RNA and proteins show what’s happening now, including the consequences of a disease and its treatment. They’re harder to read as causes.

title: Omics for Beginners
text:
Genome vocabulary








Word
Means
Example in the series




Genome
all of a person’s DNA: about 3 billion “letters” (A, C, G, T) on 23 pairs of chromosomes



Gene
a stretch of DNA with the instructions for one product
TCF7L2, on chromosome 10


Position
where a letter is: chromosome:position, on a reference genome map. All of Us uses GRCh38
chr10:112998590


Variant
a place where people’s DNA differs
rs7903146


SNP (“snip”)
a variant where one letter differs
C or T at rs7903146


Indel
a few letters inserted or deleted



STR
a short tandem repeat: a short pattern repeated a different number of times in different people. Harder to sequence
the top hit in 4.2


Allele
one version of a variant. REF = the one in the reference genome; ALT = the other(s)
REF C, ALT T


Multi-allelic
a variant with more than one ALT allele
rs7903146 is C, T, or G in All of Us


Genotype
a person’s two alleles (one from each parent), often counted as 0, 1, or 2 copies of one allele
C/T = 1 copy of T


Allele frequency
how common an allele is in a group
T: about 28% of alleles in All of Us


rsID
a standard name for a known variant. All of Us files name variants by position instead
rs7903146 = chr10:112998590:C


Linkage disequilibrium (LD)
nearby variants are inherited together, so they move together. Measured by r² from 0 to 1
why a GWAS peak has many variants


Genetic ancestry
estimated from DNA; not the same as self-reported race or ethnicity
groups afr, amr, eas, eur, mid, sas


Principal components (PCs)
a few numbers per person that summarise their genetic ancestry; used to adjust for it
PC1 to PC10 in the models

Analysis
Asks
Class

which variants are linked to one disease?
4.2, 4.3

which diseases are linked to one variant?

They’re all the same idea underneath: one regression per thing tested (per variant, disease, gene, or protein), then a correction for having done many tests.

title: Omics for Beginners
text:
Statistics you’ll meet







Term
Means




Logistic regression
a model for a yes/no outcome (diabetes: yes or no). Used in the GWAS and PheWAS


Linear regression
a model for a number (gene activity, protein level). Used for RNA and proteins


Odds ratio (OR)
from logistic regression: how the odds of the outcome change per copy of an allele. 1 = no effect; 1.25 = 25% higher odds


Beta
the effect on the log scale. For logistic regression, OR = e^beta (e.g. beta 0.22 → OR 1.25)


Log₂ scale
each step of 1 means twice as much. RNA (log-CPM) and protein (NPX) values use it. A logFC of 1 = twice as high; −1 = half


p-value
how surprising the result would be if there were no effect. Small = strong evidence


Multiple testing
testing thousands of things gives some small p-values by chance alone


Bonferroni
a strict fix: divide 0.05 by the number of tests


Genome-wide significance
p < 5 × 10⁻⁸: Bonferroni for about a million independent variants


FDR (false discovery rate, adjusted p-value)
a gentler fix used for genes and proteins: among results with FDR < 0.05, about 5% are expected to be false


Covariate
another variable in the model, to adjust for (age, sex, PCs)


Confounding
a third variable that affects both things you’re comparing, creating a misleading link. Ancestry is the classic one in genetics


Power
the chance of detecting a real effect. Small samples + small effects = low power


Selection bias
a misleading link created by how the sample was chosen (class 4.4)


Collider bias
a misleading link created by adjusting for a common effect of two things (class 4.4)

text:
Normalization: what’s done for you, and what you check
Normalization removes technical differences between samples (how deeply each was sequenced, which plate it was on), so the differences left are biological. Each data type needs something different:









Layer
Done before you get the data
What you do in class
What you check




Genotypes (4.1–4.4)
quality control of samples and variants
variant QC (frequency, missingness, Hardy-Weinberg); adjust for ancestry PCs
that the known variant replicates; the Q-Q plot


RNA counts (4.5)
reads aligned to the genome and counted per gene
normalize yourself: TMM factors (edgeR), log-CPM, voom weights
TMM factors near 1; boxplots line up after normalizing; the voom trend; PCA


Protein NPX (4.6)
plate-control and batch normalization; already on a log₂ scale
use as is (don’t normalize twice)
plates line up; how much plate explains of the main patterns; outliers; results with plate in the model









ImportantThe statistics packages don’t normalize for you



limma, used for both RNA and proteins, fits a model to whatever numbers you give it. It does not normalize. If you skip normalization, or normalize the wrong way, limma will still run and still give p-values: they’ll just be wrong. That’s why the classes show the normalization and check it, rather than hiding it in one line.

title: 4.1 Introduction to Genomic Data
text:
Overview
All of Us has sequenced the genomes of more than 535,000 participants. This class answers the first questions anyone has about that data: what is it, where is it, who has it, and how do I connect it to people’s health records? It ends with a first look at rs7903146, the variant in the gene TCF7L2 that is the strongest known genetic risk factor for type 2 diabetes.

Why this class matters
Every later genetics class (4.2–4.4) depends on what happens here: the cohort linked to genomes, the related people removed, the genetic ancestry that every model adjusts for, and a small extract of the genome that’s cheap to work with. Doing these steps carefully once, and understanding them, prevents the most common mistakes in genetic studies.


By the end you’ll be able to

Explain DNA, variants, alleles, and genotypes in plain language
Describe the All of Us genomic data and its file formats
Find the genomic files, and the ready-made ancestry and relatedness files
Link genomes to the type 2 diabetes cohort and choose a fair sample
Use PLINK 2 to extract one region of the genome, and look at one famous variant



Analysis at a glance







❓ Question
Where is the genomic data, who in our cohort has it, and is the T allele of rs7903146 more common in people with type 2 diabetes?


🧪 The analysis
Counts and allele frequencies in cases and controls; a first logistic regression of case status on the number of T alleles (unadjusted)


🎯 Why
Before any genome-wide analysis, check that the genomes link to the cohort and that a known signal shows up. Logistic regression, because the outcome is yes/no


✅ What we conclude
The direction and rough size of a well-known association, and a sample ready for 4.2


⚠️ What it can’t tell us
The effect after accounting for age, sex, and ancestry; anything about other variants; whether the variant causes diabetes


🔗 Connections
Saves the sample and files used by 4.2 and 4.3; its ancestry PCs are used in 4.2–4.4





Time and cost







⏱️ Class time
120 minutes


⏱️ Run time
about 5 minutes to run every cell. Slowest: the cohort query (1–2 minutes)


💰 Cost
about $1 to $2 per student: one BigQuery query (under $1) plus the app (about $0.27 an hour)

title: 4.1 Introduction to Genomic Data
text:
Key concepts
The essentials are below. Omics for Beginners has the full glossary.

Variants and genotypes
People’s DNA is 99.9% the same. The places where it differs are variants. At rs7903146, people have a C or a T (and, very rarely, a G). Each person has two copies (one from each parent), so their genotype is counted as 0, 1, or 2 copies of the T allele:



Genotype
Copies of T




C/C
0


C/T
1


T/T
2



Each extra copy of T raises the odds of type 2 diabetes by about 30 to 40% in large published studies. TCF7L2 affects how the pancreas releases insulin.


How the genomic files are organised
All of Us provides the genomes in several formats, one set of files per chromosome. We use the PLINK 2 format, a set of three files:
acaf_threshold.chr10.pgen   genotypes (compressed): 80 GB
acaf_threshold.chr10.pvar   the variants: one row each
acaf_threshold.chr10.psam   the people: one row each
ACAF is the subset of common variants (above about 1% frequency in at least one ancestry group).
One chromosome is 80 GB, so the class never reads a whole one: PLINK jumps to the region we need and reads only that.


Why remove related people, and adjust for ancestry?

Relatives share long stretches of DNA, which makes results look more certain than they are. All of Us provides a list of people to remove so that no two remaining people are closely related.
Genetic ancestry affects both allele frequencies and disease rates. Without accounting for it, a variant can look linked to a disease just because both are more common in one group (confounding). All of Us provides each person’s ancestry group and principal components (PCs): a few numbers that summarise their genetic ancestry, used as covariates from 4.2 on.

Code walk-through
The key steps, line by line. The notebook explains every cell; these are the ones beginners most often ask about.

Linking genomes to the cohort
1cohort <- run_query(str_glue(cohort_sql, AGE_DATE = "2025-01-01")) %>%
2  mutate(person_id = as.character(person_id))

psam <- read_tsv(file.path(pgen_dir, "acaf_threshold.chr10.psam"),
3                 col_types = cols(.default = "c"))
4genome_ids <- psam[["#IID"]]

5cohort <- cohort %>% mutate(has_genome = person_id %in% genome_ids)

1

Run the shared type 2 diabetes query (in notebooks/sql/t2d_cohort.sql), with age calculated on 2025-01-01, the v9 data cutoff.

2

Turn person_id into text. The genome files store IDs as text, and a number never matches text in R, even with the same digits.

3

Read the .psam file (one row per person with a genome), with every column as text.

4

The ID column is called #IID. The # is part of its name, so it’s written in quotes inside [[ ]].

5

%in% asks, for each person in the cohort: is your ID in the genome list? The answer (TRUE or FALSE) becomes a new column.




Choosing a fair sample
eligible <- cohort %>%
1  filter(cohort %in% c("case", "control"),
2         has_genome,
3         !person_id %in% related$sample_id,
4         between(age, 18, 100),
5         sex_at_birth %in% c("Female", "Male"))

6set.seed(2026)
gwas_samples <- eligible %>%
7  arrange(person_id) %>%
  group_by(cohort) %>%
8  slice_sample(n = 2500) %>%
  ungroup()

1

Keep cases and controls (drop the “excluded” group, e.g. people with type 1 diabetes).

2

Keep people with a genome.

3

Drop people on the relatedness list (! means “not”).

4

Ages 18 to 100: a few recorded ages above 100 are probably data errors.

5

Sex at birth is a covariate later, so it must be recorded as Female or Male.

6

Fix the random number generator, so everyone gets the same “random” sample.

7

Sort first: BigQuery doesn’t return rows in a fixed order, and the same seed only gives the same sample if the rows start in the same order.

8

Pick 2,500 at random within each group (because of group_by()).




Counting the T allele
1write_lines("chr10:112998590:C\tT", allele_file)

system(str_glue(
  "plink2 --pfile {shQuote(out_prefix)} ",
2  "--chr 10 --from-bp 112998590 --to-bp 112998590 ",
3  "--export A --export-allele {shQuote(allele_file)} ",
  "--out {shQuote(lead_prefix)}"
), intern = TRUE)

1

A one-line file: the variant’s ID and the allele to count. \t is a tab.

2

Just one position: rs7903146.

3

--export A writes each person’s genotype as 0, 1, or 2 copies of an allele. Because rs7903146 has two ALT alleles (T and G), PLINK would count the REF allele (C) by default; --export-allele tells it to count T.

TipInstructor tip: timing and pitfalls






Run Part 3’s cohort query during Part 2’s discussion if the class is short on time: it takes 1–2 minutes.
The most common error is IDs stored as numbers. If --keep: 0 samples remaining, check that person_id was turned into text before keep.txt was written.

section: AI Tools: Use Them Outside the Workbench
text:
AI Tools: Use Them Outside the Workbench
Interested in using an AI tool (e.g., Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini) for help with your code? Use it outside the Workbench, for coding help only.
Why not inside the Workbench?

All of Us does not allow participant-level data to leave the Workbench, and that includes sending it to an AI service
AI coding assistants like Claude Code can open files and run code on their own. It’s easy for them to read data files, query results, or notebook outputs that contain participant-level data.
Even one accidental read counts as a Data User Code of Conduct violation, even if nothing is stored

👉 How: get your code from GitHub (outputs cleared, no data), ask the AI on your own computer, then bring the fixed code back into your workspace






TipInstructor tip





Source: All of Us User Support Hub, “Frequently Asked Questions” (support.researchallofus.org/hc/en-us/articles/52861503885460): AI/ML tools used on participant data must run only within the Researcher Workbench, with no outgoing API; “transit of individual-level data to any external system is considered a DUCC violation, even if the data is not stored or used.” Summary statistics that follow the dissemination policy (no counts under 20) may be shared. Claude Code and Gemini CLI can be installed in Workbench apps, but both send what they read to outside services (Anthropic, Google), so this training recommends not using them there.

section: What You Can Share with an AI
text:
What You Can Share with an AI
✅ Safe to share (no participant data):

Your code, with outputs cleared
Public example code: All of Us tutorial workspace notebooks and other notebooks published by All of Us, with outputs cleared (some are saved with outputs)
Table and column names: the CDR v9 Data Dictionary or the OMOP Common Data Model documentation
Concept IDs and names from Athena or the public All of Us Data Browser, e.g. 201820 = Diabetes mellitus
Error messages, after checking they don’t include data values (an ID, a date, a result)
A small fake dataset with the same columns, to test your code. Ask the AI to make one, or use the synthetic data from Try It: Practice with Synthetic Data.

❌ Never share: query results, data files, notebook outputs, screenshots of data, participant IDs, or counts of 1 to 20.
Example prompts:

“Using these OMOP tables from the data dictionary, write a BigQuery query that finds everyone with concept 201820 or any of its descendants.”
“Here’s the All of Us tutorial notebook for loading RNA-seq data. Rewrite it in R.”
“Here’s my R code and the error message. What’s wrong?”
“Make a fake data frame with columns person_id, age, and diabetes so I can test this code.”







TipInstructor tip





Source: All of Us User Support Hub, “Data Dictionaries” (https://support.researchallofus.org/hc/en-us/articles/360033200232-Data-Dictionaries), which links the data dictionary for each CDR version. Everything in the safe list contains no participant data. Error messages are the one to check: some quote a value from the data.

Participant-centered: participants can view and access their own data
Open science: de-identified data available to registered researchers
Research opportunities: health disparities, environmental impacts, disease prevention and treatment
Phenotypic and genotypic data in one place
Scalability and innovation: complex analyses, AI and machine learning

title: About All of Us
text:
Data Sources










Source
Description
Participants (v9)





Surveys
Lifestyle, medical and family history, health care access, social factors
> 747,000



EHR
Diagnoses, medications, labs, procedures, and visits from health care providers, standardized with the OMOP Common Data Model
> 481,000



Physical measurements
Height, weight, blood pressure, heart rate, and waist and hip measured at enrollment visits
> 600,000



Wearables
Steps, heart rate, and sleep (including sleep stages) from Fitbit; some Apple HealthKit data
> 68,000 (Fitbit)



Genomic
Short-read and long-read whole genomes, and genotyping arrays, from blood or saliva
> 535,000 (short-read)



Multi-omics (new in v9)
RNA-seq from whole blood; proteomics from plasma
about 9,000 each



Clinical notes (new in v9)
Conditions extracted from clinical notes; a separate Controlled Tier release, not in the main tables
> 99,000



Not available: medical images (e.g. X-rays, MRI or CT scans). EHR procedure records only show that an imaging exam happened (e.g. radiologic examination of knee) and when; some of these codes are removed for privacy.






TipInstructor tip





Source: All of Us Researcher Workbench Office Hours, “Release of the Curated Data Repository (CDR) v9 Dataset” (2026-07-24), and the CDR v9 data dictionary. Counts change with every release. EHR data now comes from health care sites, from records participants share themselves, and from a health-information-exchange pilot. To verify on the Support Hub before relying on them: whether physical measurements also include self-reported height and weight, and the exact sample types used for DNA. Medical imaging (X-rays, MRI, CT) is not part of v9: the data dictionary has no imaging tables, and the v9 release talk doesn’t list it among current or upcoming data types. EHR procedure records only show that an imaging exam happened.

title: About All of Us
text:
The Curated Data Repository (CDR)

Data are organized in a curated data repository (CDR), released in numbered versions (current: CDR v9; refreshed every 1–2 years)

Participant identifiers removed; the Controlled Tier keeps more detail (e.g. real dates of health events)
Cleaned, validated, and standardized to the OMOP Common Data Model

Researcher Workbench 2.0 runs on Verily Workbench, on Google Cloud

Tables (EHR, surveys, measurements, Fitbit) are in Google BigQuery: query them with SQL from R or Python, or with the Data Explorer
Genomic and multi-omics data are files in Cloud Storage buckets (e.g. PLINK, VCF, Hail formats)

Costs go to your Google Cloud billing account: BigQuery charges by the data a query scans, apps by the hour while running, and the genomic data bucket is Requester Pays (reading it is billed to you)







TipInstructor tip





CDRv9 is shown on the Workbench 2.0 home page (Controlled Tier tutorial workspace). Verily builds and runs Workbench 2.0; the data and computing are on Google Cloud. Version 9 of the Controlled Tier is the dataset C2025Q4R6.

title: Research Use Statement
text: When you add an All of Us data collection to a workspace (see Setting Up a Workspace), you answer these questions about your research. Our example answers are for an instructional workspace.

title: Research Use Statement
text:
Research Use Statement: Question 1










What is the primary purpose of your project?

Research
Education ← our example (instructional workspace)
For-profit
Other

8 pages of questions in total
Answer for your own project. Answers marked Publicly displayed appear in the Research Hub Directory.








TipInstructor tip





This example workspace is for teaching, so we answer as an education project. Students doing research should choose Research purpose and describe their actual project.

title: Research Use Statement
text:
Research Use Statement: Question 2





Summarize your research purpose in plain language:

2.1 Your scientific question(s), and why they matter
2.2 Your approach: datasets, methods, and tools
2.3 Your anticipated findings

Each answer: 100–1,000 characters
⚠️ Answers under 100 characters give an error. Add enough detail to explain your project.








TipInstructor tip





Example answer for this instructional workspace (used for 2.1–2.3): “This workspace is intended solely for instructional purposes and not for research. I will use this workspace to teach others how to navigate the All of Us Workbench, create workspaces, build cohorts and datasets, and analyze the data provided within the workbench.” Students should describe their real project: hypothesis, methods, and expected findings, with as little jargon as possible.

title: Research Use Statement
text:
Research Use Statement: Question 3










How will you share your findings?

Choose all that apply: journals, conferences, community forums, social media, blogs, press…
Name the venue if you know it (journal, conference, blog, etc.)
Other requires a short explanation

Our example: Other. The workspace is for teaching, so there are no findings to share.








TipInstructor tip





All of Us encourages sharing results with both scientific and community audiences, to recognize participants’ contributions. Example answer: “The purpose of this workspace is to provide instruction, not research. I do not plan on disseminating anything from the work done here.”

title: Research Use Statement
text:
Research Use Statement: Question 4










How does your project fit the All of Us Scientific Framework?
Select all outcomes you expect:

Wellness, resilience, healthy living
Health equity for underrepresented (UBR) populations
Risk assessment and prevention
Earlier, more accurate diagnosis
Better treatment and precision interventions

Our example: None of these apply (teaching workspace)

title: Research Use Statement
text:
Research Use Statement: Question 5










Population of interest: will your study focus on historically underrepresented populations?

Yes: select the groups, e.g., race/ethnicity, age, sex at birth, gender identity, sexual orientation, geography, disability, access to care, education, income
No: a diverse sample in general, or well-represented populations

Our example: No (teaching workspace)








TipInstructor tip





All of Us asks this to track how well it serves underrepresented communities and to guard against stigmatizing findings. Encourage students to think about whether their design, methods, or analyses could harm individuals, groups, or communities. Fields marked * are altered, suppressed, or generalized in the Registered Tier for privacy; see the Data Dictionary.

title: Research Use Statement
text:
Research Use Statement: Question 6










AI/AN Policy Assessment
Will your study produce findings specific to American Indian and Alaska Native (AI/AN) populations?

AI/AN-only study population
AI/AN case or control group
Results broken down so AI/AN-specific findings may appear
No AI/AN-specific analyses

Then explain your answer (required)
Our example: no AI/AN-specific analyses. If that changes, you must update your answers.








TipInstructor tip





All of Us has a policy on respectful research with AI/AN populations; this question checks whether it applies to your project. Students whose work could produce AI/AN-specific findings should read the policy before starting.

title: Research Use Statement
text:
Research Use Statement: Question 7













Request a review of your research purpose?

Research using demographic variables can unintentionally produce findings that stigmatize participants or communities
You can ask the Resource Access Board (RAB) to review your purpose

Reply within 5 business days; keep working meanwhile

This answer is private (not on the Research Hub)

Our example: No concerns. The RAB is available any time via the User Support Hub.








TipInstructor tip





See the All of Us Stigmatizing Research Policy for more detail. If students are unsure, encourage them to request the review; it’s a precaution, not a penalty.

title: Research Use Statement
text:
Research Use Statement: Page 8













Review and confirm
These answers are publicly displayed to inform All of Us participants:

Q1 Primary purpose of your project
Q2 Summary of research purpose
Q5 Population of interest
Q6 Approach to handling AI/AN data

Check that they’re detailed and in plain language, then click Confirm
You can go Back to change answers now, or edit them later after the workspace is created








TipInstructor tip





Q3 (dissemination), Q4 (scientific framework), and Q7 (RAB review) are not displayed publicly.

title: Setting Up a Workspace
text: This page uses our example workspace, intro-to-AoU, created for instruction only.

title: Setting Up a Workspace
text:
Creating a Workspace
Left sidebar → Workspaces → + New workspace












TipInstructor tip





Three steps: Enter details → Set policies → Add description.

title: Setting Up a Workspace
text:
Step 1: Enter Details





You fill in:

Workspace name: only visible to people with access; you can change it later
Summary: a short description (up to 140 characters)

Filled in automatically:

Workspace ID: made from the name; used by the CLI. Changing it later breaks links to the workspace.
Pod: your default billing pod

Click Next
⚠️ The pod can’t be changed after the workspace is created








TipInstructor tip





The auto-selected pod is your personal user pod (user-pod-firstname-lastname-####). If you’ve set up a Yale billing pod, choose it here from the drop-down.

title: Setting Up a Workspace
text:
Step 2: Set Policies





Sharing (group policy):

No, don’t apply policy: the default; fine for most projects
Limit discoverability: only members of the selected groups can see the workspace

Region:

Where your apps and resources are kept. Pick the one closest to you (Yale: us-east4).
Can be changed later; only new resources use it

Click Next
⚠️ Group policies can’t be removed once applied








TipInstructor tip





Group policies also carry over to duplicates of the workspace. Access still has to be granted separately; a group policy only limits who can be given access. Region also affects cost: Verily notes prices can vary by about 25% between regions. Yale is on the East Coast, so us-east4 (Virginia) is the closest region.

title: Setting Up a Workspace
text:
Step 3: Add Description





Description:

What the workspace is for: its purpose, data, and tools
Helps you and your collaborators
You can edit it any time

Click Create workspace
⚠️ The description is publicly accessible. Anyone can see it, so don’t put sensitive details in it.

title: Setting Up a Workspace
text:
Your New Workspace
Go to the Resources tab → + Data from catalog















TipInstructor tip





Workspace tabs: Overview, Resources (data and cloud storage), Apps (JupyterLab, RStudio, SAS…), Workflows. Edit and Share are at the top right. A new workspace starts with 0 resources and 0 active policies; the policies come in when you add a data collection.

title: Setting Up a Workspace
text:
Adding a Data Collection
A new workspace has no data until you add a data collection.
Resources tab → + Data from catalog (or Add to workspace on the Exchange), then:

Select collection: All of Us Registered Tier or Controlled Tier
Select resource: e.g., the CDR version
Review policies: answer the Researcher Use Statement questions
Review selection → Add to your workspace

title: Setting Up a Workspace
text:
Step 1: Select Collection











Pick the collection you need. Here: All of Us Controlled Tier
You add references: pointers to the existing data

No copying or data migration
The source data isn’t affected

Status column:

Perimeter required: adding it puts a security perimeter on your workspace
✅ No extra policy needed (e.g., GTEx)


Click Next








TipInstructor tip





Only collections you have access to appear here (the same list as your Data collections page). The GCP filter is on by default.

Step 2: Select Resources











The collection version (cdrv9) holds 9 resources
Choose some or all. Here: Select all resources
Two kinds of resources:

BigQuery datasets: data tables you query with SQL
Cloud Storage buckets/objects: files, e.g., genomic data


Click Next

The Controlled Tier has 6 policies, including:

Research Use Statement: click Fill out the questions. You can’t continue until it’s complete.

⚠️ Your answers are public in the Research Hub Directory

The answers aren’t used to make data access decisions; they’re for transparency to participants. All of Us expects a separate workspace for each project, so the answers should be specific to this project. Scroll down in the dialog to see all 6 policies.

Answer the Research Use Statement
Adding an All of Us data collection asks you to answer the Research Use Statement questions. They’re covered step by step on their own page: Research Use Statement.

Step 3: Confirm Policies

Group policy: collaborators must be in the All of Us Controlled Tier group

Bucket browsing in the perimeter: previews up to 5 MB, and only .ipynb, .r, .rmd, and .sas files can be viewed. The group is P_b_aou-prod-ct, so collaborators need Controlled Tier access too.

title: Setting Up a Workspace

Step 4: Review Selection

Missing something? Go Back

The resources then appear in your workspace’s Resources tab. Allow up to 30 min for the perimeter enrollment to finish.

title: Setting Up a Workspace
text:
Data Collection Rules

title: Workflows
text:
What Is a Workflow?
A pipeline that runs analysis steps for you, in order or in parallel, without an app running. Each step runs in its own container on a temporary cloud machine.
Use it when you need to: run the same analysis on many files or samples (e.g., genomics), or make it easy to reproduce and share



Tool
Language
Where you run it




Cromwell
WDL
Workflows tab (or CLI)


Nextflow
Nextflow (.nf)
Workflows tab (or CLI)


dsub
Shell commands, one step
An app’s terminal



👉 Most class projects don’t need workflows: an app is enough. Ready-made workflows: Dockstore






TipInstructor tip





Source: Verily, “Workflows overview” and “Workflow engines”. All three tools use the Google Batch API to run tasks, and read and write files in buckets (gs:// paths). Tasks run with the workspace’s service account, which can access every bucket in the workspace. Costs (task machines and storage) are billed to the workspace’s pod and are not shown in the app cost estimator.

title: Workflows
text:
Adding a Workflow
















Step 1: Provide source. Where’s the workflow file?

Workspace bucket: pick the bucket. Workbench lists the workflow files it finds there (search by name).
Git repository: a repo with the workflow (see the GitHub guide)

Select the workflow → Next
Step 2: Review details → add it
Upload the workflow file (.wdl or .nf) to your bucket first. Until there’s one to select, Next stays grey.








TipInstructor tip





The bucket shown (dataproc-staging-aou-rw-…) is the staging bucket created for a Spark (Dataproc) app; your own bucket appears in the same list. Nextflow workflows should include a nextflow.config file next to the .nf file.

title: Workflows
text:
Running a Workflow
Setup tab → select the workflow → + New job

Fill in the inputs. Workbench builds the form from the workflow file.
Choose an output bucket for the results
Start the job, then follow it on Job status: each task’s progress, logs, and outputs

Batch jobs: run one WDL workflow many times in parallel, e.g., once per sample

Choose Run a batch job with inputs defined by an input table
Upload a CSV (one row per run), then match its columns to the workflow’s inputs







TipInstructor tip





Source: Verily, “Use the Cromwell engine to run WDL workflows” and “Create batch jobs”. Cromwell call caching is on by default, so re-running reuses results from steps that already finished. Limits: 1,000 outstanding jobs per user and 5,000 submitted in 24 hours; for a batch, the limit applies to each job, and a batch that exceeds it is rejected entirely. Genomic Variant Store (GVS) is an example of a large WDL workflow from the Broad Institute; Verily has a guide for it.

title: Workflows
text:
dsub: Jobs from an App
For one-step jobs, e.g., run a command on many files. It comes with apps created after June 2025.
dsub_activate                        # turn on dsub in the terminal

dsub \
  --provider google-batch \
  --project "${GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT}" \
  --service-account "${PET_SA_EMAIL}" \
  --logging gs://<your-bucket>/logs/ \
  --input  BAM=gs://<your-bucket>/sample.bam \
  --output BAI=gs://<your-bucket>/sample.bam.bai \
  --image  <container image with samtools> \
  --command 'samtools index ${BAM} ${BAI}' \
  --wait
👉 More examples: tutorial notebook 05_How_to_use_workflow_tools (dsub, Cromwell, Nextflow)






TipInstructor tip





Source: Verily, “Run dsub jobs”. Verily’s example also sets the network and subnetwork; check the tutorial notebook for the exact flags in an All of Us workspace. Each dsub job starts its own cloud machine, billed to your pod.





Next section: Data →
